lines: \paragraph{Synthetic validation.} On synthetic data ($N = 50$, 20 seeds), G-MFRM reduces ability RMSE by 51\% relative to sequential estimation ($p < 10^{-6}$) and improves ranking accuracy ($\tau$: $0.922$ vs.\ $0.839$, Wilcoxon $p < 0.001$). Contamination susceptibility is recovered with Pearson $r = 0.81$.

-\paragraph{Predictive fit.} In the $N = 8$ pilot, LOO cross-validation strongly favors G-MFRM over MFRM-only ($\Delta\mathrm{ELPD}_{\mathrm{LOO}} = -55.7$, SE $= 9.4$, $|\Delta/\mathrm{SE}| = 5.9$; \citealp{vehtari2017loo}), with stacking weight 1.0 and all Pareto $\hat{k} < 0.7$ (Appendix~\ref{app:loo_comparison}).

+\paragraph{Predictive fit.} In the $N = 8$ pilot, LOO cross-validation strongly favors G-MFRM over MFRM-only (Expected Log Pointwise Predictive Density difference $\Delta\mathrm{ELPD}_{\mathrm{LOO}} = -55.7$, SE $= 9.4$, $|\Delta/\mathrm{SE}| = 5.9$; \citealp{vehtari2017loo}), with stacking weight 1.0 and all Pareto $\hat{k} < 0.7$ (Appendix~\ref{app:loo_comparison}).

\paragraph{Reconciling predictive fit and ranking accuracy.} The LOO improvement and the ranking degradation are not contradictory: they measure different quantities. LOO-ELPD evaluates observation-level predictive accuracy across all $(n, i, j)$ triples, rewarding the model for capturing contamination structure in individual responses. Kendall $\tau$ evaluates aggregate system-level rankings, which are sensitive to the accuracy of per-item exposure estimates $e_i$. The separation indicates that the contamination signal is real (the model fits better), but incomplete exposure coverage causes the correction to over-correct when aggregated to rankings. The coverage ablation below confirms this interpretation.

In the $N = 8$ pilot, the contamination susceptibility profile (Figure~\ref{fig:contamination_and_bias}a) reveals a clear gradient by model age: older models show $\hat{c}_n > 4$ (GPT-3.5-Turbo: $5.60$; GPT-4-0613: $4.20$), while recent models show near-zero susceptibility (GPT-4o: $0.88$; GPT-4o-mini: $0.93$). MFRM-only estimation absorbs this contamination signal into ability estimates, inflating $\hat{\theta}$ for the most contaminated models by up to 0.79 logits (Figure~\ref{fig:contamination_and_bias}b; Spearman $\rho = 1.0$ between $\hat{c}_n$ and $\Delta\theta$, though with only $N = 8$ data points, perfect rank correlation is not statistically remarkable and should not be interpreted as a robust finding). The $N = 17$ analysis preserves the same age gradient at lower absolute scale (GPT-3.5-Turbo: $2.57$; GPT-4-0613: $3.78$), consistent with shrinkage from the larger model population. All parameters achieve $\hat{R} \leq 1.003$ with ESS $\geq 1{,}240$ in the $N = 8$ pilot (Appendices~\ref{app:item_diagnostics} and~\ref{app:ppc}).

4	We introduced G-MFRM, a Bayesian measurement model that jointly estimates model ability, judge severity, and contamination susceptibility within a single inferential framework. The key theoretical contribution is formalizing the confounding between judge bias and benchmark contamination as omitted variable bias: omitting the contamination facet produces systematic bias in ability estimates, driven primarily by the specification error itself rather than the exposure-severity covariance (Section~\ref{sec:confounding}).
5	
6	On Arena-Hard, G-MFRM provides interpretable per-model contamination diagnostics unavailable from existing methods: older models exhibit 4--6$\times$ higher susceptibility, and MFRM-only estimation inflates ability for the most contaminated models by up to 0.79 logits. A controlled coverage ablation ($\Delta\tau$: $-0.044 \to -0.015 \to 0.000$ as coverage increases to 100\%) demonstrates that over-correction is attributable to incomplete exposure estimation, and complete coverage eliminates the over-correction observed in partial-coverage settings. Ablation confirms joint estimation as the dominant contributor: staged estimation doubles ability RMSE.

8	Two practical implications emerge. First, evaluation frameworks that treat judge bias and contamination as independent incur systematic errors; future LLM evaluation should model these facets jointly. Second, the coverage--degradation finding provides an actionable quality requirement for contamination-aware evaluation. Several directions remain open: higher-rank contamination decompositions for domain-specific effects, simulation-based recalibration \citep{talts2018sbc} of $c_n$ credible intervals (71\% coverage at nominal 95\%), and scaling to larger model populations and diverse benchmarks.

Two practical implications emerge. First, evaluation frameworks that treat judge bias and contamination as independent incur systematic errors; future LLM evaluation should model these facets jointly. Second, the coverage--degradation finding provides an actionable quality requirement for contamination-aware evaluation. For practitioners operating Arena-style evaluations, G-MFRM can serve as a post-hoc calibration layer: given pairwise judgments and exposure estimates, the model produces contamination-adjusted rankings and flags models warranting training data audits. The exposure estimation pipeline (\S\ref{sec:staged}) is modular, so improved contamination detectors---whether based on membership inference, output perturbation, or direct training data access---can substitute for the current reference-anchoring approach without modifying the measurement model.

Several directions remain open: higher-rank contamination decompositions for domain-specific effects, simulation-based recalibration \citep{talts2018sbc} of $c_n$ credible intervals (71\% coverage at nominal 95\%), and scaling to larger model populations and diverse benchmarks.

file.content: The evaluation uses a single benchmark (Arena-Hard) with an incomplete observation design (${\sim}$58\% fill rate); generalization to other benchmarks and larger model populations remains to be verified. Posterior credible intervals for contamination susceptibility $c_n$ exhibit systematic overconfidence (71\% coverage at nominal 95\%; Appendix~\ref{app:ci_coverage}), a structural issue from the multiplicative coupling and HalfNormal boundary at $c_n = 0$ that warrants simulation-based recalibration. The rank-1 contamination structure assumes a single $c_n$ per model, whereas contamination may be domain-specific (e.g., coding vs.\ reasoning), motivating higher-rank decompositions in future work. The judge panel comprises six models from four provider families; whether G-MFRM's severity separation generalizes to larger or more homogeneous panels (e.g., multiple versions of the same model family) is untested. Finally, exposure estimation relies on reference model anchoring with a fixed anchor (GPT-4-0314); anchor choice may introduce systematic bias in $e_i$ estimates, particularly for items where the anchor's own training data overlaps with the benchmark.
